messages.subject: DSM
parts:
Hi all, 
I am running a DSM and I have a few questions. 

1) As I understood in order to choose the basis complexity (k) I need to increase k and see at what value of k the edf stabilize. Right? 

2) I was reading choose.k from mgcv package. 
"A useful general purpose approach goes as follows: (i) fit your model and extract the deviance residuals; (ii) for each smooth term in your model, fit an equivalent, single, smooth to the residuals, using a substantially increased k to see if there is a pattern in the residuals that could potentially be explained by increasing k". I am doing this but I am first fitting the model without the smoothed parameter. The residuals have a huge amount of zeros, so I would use a Tweedie response distribution. I also use a Tweedie in the first model. The obvious issue is that being residuals they are not positive.  
What response distribution should I choose to fit the residuals? Should I transform them? 
Thank you very much

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DSM
parts:
Hi Valentina, hi listfolk,

Some inline responses below (with apologies for the tardy reply)...

On 10/12/2017 22:39, Valentina Zini wrote:
> Hi all,
> I am running a DSM and I have a few questions.
>
> 1) As I understood in order to choose the basis complexity (k) I need to
> increase k and see at what value of k the edf stabilize. Right?

"Stabilize" in the sense that if the EDF is close to k, I would double k
and see if there is a big change in the EDF in the refitted model.

> 2) I was reading choose.k from mgcv package.
> "A useful general purpose approach goes as follows: (i) fit your model
> and extract the deviance residuals; (ii) for each smooth term in your
> model, fit an equivalent, single, smooth to the residuals, using a
> substantially increased k to see if there is a pattern in the residuals
> that could potentially be explained by increasing k". I am doing this
> but I am first fitting the model without the smoothed parameter. The
> residuals have a huge amount of zeros, so I would use a Tweedie response
> distribution. I also use a Tweedie in the first model. The obvious issue
> is that being residuals they are not positive.
> What response distribution should I choose to fit the residuals? Should
> I transform them?

Indeed, Tweedie is a good choice for most DSMs. For fitting to the
residuals, the deviance residuals should be normally distributed if the
model is correct (see, e.g., p. 113 of Wood, 2017 or any other text on
GLMs/GAMs). Therefore no transformation is necessary.

Hope this helps.

cheers,
--dave



References

Wood, SN. (2017) Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R,
Second Edition.
